Title: The Wheat on the Chessboard
Author: by Liz Huyck
Content: Long ago in India, there was a wise mathematician called Sessa. He invented a new game to amuse his friend, the king. He called it “chess.” The king loved chess and told Sessa to name anything he liked as his reward. Anything! The king enjoyed boasting of his limitless wealth. But instead of gold, jewels, or elephants, after much thought Sessa told the king that he wished only some grains of wheat.

“I am a simple man,” replied Sessa, “and my wants are few. But since you enjoy my chessboard so much, give me a `text(single)` grain of wheat on the `text(first)` square, `text(two)` grains on the `text(second)` square, `text(four)` for the `text(third)`, and so on. For `text(each square)` `text(double)` the last, as `text(each day)` of play `text(doubles)` our delight. That will mean more to me than all the riches in the world.”
“Very well!” said the king, a little irritated, thinking that Sessa was mocking him. “If wheat is all he wants,” he told his treasurer, “give it to him!”
The `text(first day)`, the treasurer presented Sessa with a `text(single)` grain of wheat, to the huge amusement of the court.
The `text(second day)`, he got `text(two)`, on a little cushion. The great lords roared with laughter. But Sessa kept his thoughts to himself.

On the `text(ninth day)`, Sessa received `256` grains, enough to make a small handful. But the very next `text(day)`, he had `text(two)` handfuls. It took Sessa `text(16 days)` to get enough wheat to fill a large bag. But only `text(one)` more day to get `text(two)` bags. The `text(day)` after, he had `text(four)` bags.
The courtiers stopped laughing and started whispering.
By the end of the `text(month)`, wagons filled with grain were rumbling toward Sessa’s house, and the treasurer began to look worried. Quaking in his boots, he went to see the king.

“Highness!” he trembled. “Please look over my calculations, but I don’t think they are in error. By his simple `text(doubling)`, Sessa has now collected nearly all our stores of wheat! What shall we do? If we continue at this rate the treasury will soon be empty, and I doubt there is enough wheat in the entire world to pay him!”

“Impossible!” said the king. But he checked and `text(double-checked)` the sums, and there was no doubt. In horror, he saw that by square `64`, he would owe Sessa a total of `text(18,446,744,073,709,551,615)` grains of wheat!
He could not even imagine so many grains— they would make a pile of wheat larger than the tallest mountain. That much wheat could not be gathered in all of India for the next `text(2,000 years)`!
There was nothing for the king to do but call Sessa, and take back his boasts of limitless wealth.
“Sire!” Sessa replied. “Say no more. I am happy with what I have already — I forgive you the `text(second half)` of the chessboard.”

With that, the king and Sessa remained the best of friends and enjoyed many games of chess together. And the clever Sessa got the real reward he had wanted all along — a wiser and more mathematical king.
